title: Café Touba, Filtered with Boiling Water
author: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity (recipe), via Au Sénégal, le cœur du Sénégal
desc: 50 g of ready-made café Touba powder wet with a splash of water, set in a cloth or paper filter over a sieve, and filtered with a litre of boiling water; reheated if it cools, sweetened at the cup.
longDesc: The one full weighed recipe for café Touba, published on Au Sénégal under the title ‘Le café Touba, café « saf »’ (published 9 December 2014, modified 28 January 2023) and credited to Slow Food’s ‘Sénégal de la terre à la table’. It begins from ready-made café Touba powder — a coffee-and-djar blend — so it contains no roasting, grinding or djar ratio. The water is boiled; the powder is placed on a firm cloth tied over a container, or in a coffee filter set in a sieve, and the boiling water poured through to filter a liquid coffee. If it cools during filtering it is reheated; it is sweetened at the moment of drinking. THE PAGE PRINTS ‘1,2 litre d’eau (1 litre d’eau pour le café et 20 ml pour mouiller la poudre)’: 1 litre plus 20 millilitres is not 1.2 litres. Both figures are reported as printed and neither is corrected.
ingredients: 50 g café Touba powder (ready-made blend of coffee and djar)
1.2 litres water (printed ‘1,2 litre’) — the parenthetical reads ‘1 litre for the coffee and 20 ml to wet the powder’, which does not add up
equipment: Firm cloth tied over a container, or a coffee filter in a sieve
steps: Place the coffee powder on a firm cloth tied over a container, or tip it into a coffee filter set in a sieve. Wet the powder with the small amount of water the page specifies (20 ml as printed in the parenthesis).
Pour the boiling water through and let it filter to obtain a liquid coffee.
Reheat the coffee if it cools during filtering. Sweeten to taste when drinking.
chefTips: The page’s only cue is that the coffee should be a ‘café liquide’ once filtered; no timing is printed.
Reheat rather than leave it to cool during filtering.
Sweeten at the cup, not in the pot.
commonMistakes: Reading the water as a clean 1.2 litres.
Pouring all the water at once through a fine cloth.
reheating: The page says to reheat if it cools during filtering.
healthBenefits: Contains caffeine; djar adds a peppery warmth. No intake figures are printed in this source.
culturalNote: Café Touba is tied to the Mouride brotherhood and to the city of Touba; the recipe’s origin is attributed to the founder, Cheikh Amadou Bamba, who brought coffee back from Gabon after his exile (1902 in the sources reached). Several sources record a devotional frame around its preparation (a blessing recited over the powder is recorded on one page of uncertain authorship); this entry cites none of that detail.
sources: Title as printed: ‘Le café Touba, café « saf »’. Byline as printed: ‘le cœur du Sénégal’ (publication ‘Au Sénégal, le cœur du Sénégal’; a portal byline, flagged). Published 2014-12-09, modified 2023-01-28. Recipe credit as printed: ‘Sénégal de la terre à la table, produits et plats traditionnels’, Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity. Heading ‘Pour un litre de café Touba’. TWO-PASS, identical both passes including the arithmetic error.

SUSPECTED MISPRINT, as printed, NOT corrected: ‘1,2 litre d’eau (1 litre d’eau pour le café et 20 ml pour mouiller la poudre)’. 1 litre + 20 ml = 1.02 litres. The likely intended figure for wetting the powder may be 200 ml, but that is the compiler’s inference and is NOT source text.
ABSENT: the sugar quantity; times; any roasting, grinding or djar-to-coffee ratio (the powder is bought ready-made). The 5 and 10 minute figures are scheduling estimates.

UNRECONCILED, djar proportion in other printings (see SEN108): 2:1 coffee to ground pepper by weight (Dakaractu, 11 April 2022); about 80:20 (Wikipedia, citing BBC Afrique 2012); 10 to 15 pods to 40 g coffee (ileauxepices.com, no confirmed byline); 10 g Selim to 40 g coffee (Barista Magazine, Sandra Elisa Loofbourow, no date); no ratio given by four other Senegalese outlets.
